589.title: Against harm
589.hook: a prayer against those who seek to harm; teachers stress praying against evil, not people
589.howItsDone: The twelfth blessing of the weekday Amidah, against slanderers and wickedness, appears in different wordings in different prayer books; many teachers explain it through Beruriah's reading that the prayer is for sins to end, not sinners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer for fair judges. Your line was restore justice. Were you the fair judge in one small decision? Today, the hardest blessing in the Amidah to say well. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

A group of thugs lives in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood. The Talmud doesn't say exactly what they did, only that they caused him a great deal of trouble. And Rabbi Meir, one of the great teachers of the Mishnah, does what plenty of us would do. He prays that they die. His wife, Beruriah, hears him. She's a scholar in her own right, one of the few women the Talmud quotes on points of law. And she asks him a question about a verse.
screen: `THUGS IN THE NEIGHBORHOOD.` → `RABBI MEIR PRAYS THEY DIE.` → `BERURIAH ASKS ABOUT A VERSE.`

segments.voice: The twelfth blessing of the weekday Amidah is a prayer against those who do harm. The Talmud, in Berakhot 28b, says it was added later than the others: Rabban Gamliel asked who could compose it, and Shmuel the Small stood up and did. That's how the eighteen blessings became nineteen. Its wording has changed many times over the centuries, and scholars still debate exactly whom it first meant. Today it asks that slanderers have no hope, that wickedness vanish, and it ends: blessed are You, who breaks enemies and humbles the arrogant. It's a prayer born of real danger. So how should it be said? Back to Beruriah, in Berakhot 10a. She points to Psalm 104. In the old Jewish translation: "Let sinners cease out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more." But the Hebrew letters for sinners, she says, can also be read as sins. Let sins cease. And then, she says, look at the second half: if the sins are gone, the wicked will be no more, because they'll no longer be wicked. Pray that they turn around. Rabbi Meir does. And the Talmud says they did. That story has shaped how many teachers read this blessing ever since. Even with real enemies, the target is the harm, not the person who might still change. The wish is not for people to vanish, but for the harm to end.
screen: `THE BLESSING ADDED LATER.` · `EIGHTEEN BECOME NINETEEN.` · `SINNERS, OR SINS?` · `PRAY THAT THEY TURN AROUND.` · then, large: `END THE HARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray against one harm. Settle, and breathe. Think of one harm in your world: a bully at school, a cruel post going around, someone who keeps hurting someone you love, a wrong in the news. Let yourself feel the anger honestly. Then try Beruriah's move. Separate the harm from the person. Hold the wish that the harm stop, and, if you can manage it, that the person doing it turn around. If you pray, you can ask for that. The bell holds the time.
Against harm. The Amidah's twelfth blessing, the one added at Yavneh, read through Beruriah: let sins cease, not sinners.
Your line: end the harm. Today, when you're angry at someone, aim the anger at what they did, not at who they are. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

590.title: For the ones who chose
590.hook: a blessing for the righteous, the pious and sincere converts
590.howItsDone: Al hatzaddikim is the thirteenth blessing of the weekday Amidah, praying for the righteous, the pious, the elders, the scholars and righteous converts; converts to Judaism say the Amidah with the same words, God of our fathers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing against harm, and Beruriah's let sins cease. Your line was end the harm. Did you aim your anger at the deed, not the person? Today, the blessing that comes right after it, for the good. Day five hundred ninety.

A man named Obadiah, who has become a Jew, writes a letter to Moses Maimonides, in Egypt. His question is about the Amidah. Every day, it begins: our God and God of our fathers, God of Abraham. But Obadiah's fathers weren't Abraham's children. Should he change the words? Say God of your fathers? Or say nothing at that line at all? Is he saying something untrue three times a day? Maimonides' answer is still read today.
screen: `A LETTER TO MAIMONIDES.` → `GOD OF OUR FATHERS?` → `SOMETHING UNTRUE, THREE TIMES A DAY?`

segments.voice: Maimonides writes back: say it exactly as written. Abraham is your father too. He's the father of everyone who comes under the wings of the Divine Presence. By custom, converts are named son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah. And in the thirteenth blessing of the Amidah, the community names them in its prayer. It says: on the righteous, on the pious, on the elders of Your people, on the remnant of their scholars, on the righteous converts, and on us, may Your compassion be stirred. Give good reward to all who truly trust in Your name, and place our portion with them. Blessed are You, support and trust of the righteous. Look at that list. The converts, gerei hatzedek, stand right next to the righteous and the scholars. And notice the last item: and on us. The ordinary person praying adds themselves at the end of the list, hoping to belong in that company. The Torah tells Israel to love the stranger, the ger, a word the rabbis also use for a convert. In the old Jewish translation: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." And Ruth, whom tradition remembers as a convert, says to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Her great-grandson is King David. In this blessing, the people who chose stand in the community's daily prayer, right beside the righteous.
screen: `MAIMONIDES: ABRAHAM IS YOUR FATHER.` · `THE RIGHTEOUS, THE PIOUS, THE CONVERTS.` · `AND ON US.` · `RUTH: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `FOR THE ONES WHO CHOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who chose this path. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who chose to join a people, a family or a community they weren't born into. Maybe a convert you know. Maybe an in-law who learned all the family recipes, or a neighbor who became a citizen. Think of what it cost them: the learning, the questions, the moments of feeling outside. Hold them with respect for a few breaths. If you pray, you can include them in this blessing. The bell holds the time.
For the ones who chose. The Amidah's thirteenth blessing, for the righteous, the pious, the scholars, the righteous converts, and us.
screen: `FOR THE ONES WHO CHOSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for the ones who chose. Today, tell the person you pictured one specific thing you admire about how they joined in. Day five hundred ninety.

591.title: Jerusalem rebuilt
591.hook: blessings for Jerusalem and for the line of David
591.howItsDone: The weekday Amidah's fourteenth blessing prays for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the fifteenth for the branch of David; on the afternoon of Tisha b'Av the paragraph Nachem, a prayer of comfort, is added to the Jerusalem blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing that names the righteous converts. Your line was for the ones who chose. Did you tell someone what you admire about how they joined in? Today, a city and a family line. Day five hundred ninety-one.

At the end of a Jewish wedding, just before the cheering, the groom stamps on a glass wrapped in cloth. It shatters, and everyone shouts mazel tov. Many explain the broken glass as a memory of Jerusalem's destroyed Temple, brought into the middle of the celebration. Even here, the city is remembered. Three times a day, in the middle of the Amidah, there's a prayer that does the opposite of breaking. It asks for the city to be built.
screen: `A GLASS UNDER THE GROOM'S FOOT.` → `JERUSALEM, EVEN AT A WEDDING.` → `A PRAYER THAT BUILDS.`

segments.voice: The fourteenth blessing says: to Jerusalem, Your city, return in mercy, and dwell in it as You promised. Rebuild it soon, in our days, as an everlasting building, and quickly set up the throne of David within it. Blessed are You, who builds Jerusalem. Notice the tense of the ending. Not who will build, or who built. Who builds: an ongoing act, a work site that never closes. The fifteenth blessing goes on to the family of David: may the branch of David Your servant sprout soon, for we hope for Your salvation all day long. Blessed are You, who makes the horn of salvation sprout. Branch, sprout: the Hebrew is tzemach, a prophets' image for a king from David's line, whom Jewish tradition calls mashiach, the anointed one, the messiah. Reform Judaism has generally spoken instead of a messianic age, a repaired world, rather than one person; Orthodox Judaism keeps the hope of a king from David's line. Some early prayer texts found in the Cairo Geniza show that in the land of Israel these two were once a single blessing. And the Psalms have a simple instruction about this city. In the old Jewish translation: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." On the afternoon of the fast of Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, a special paragraph of comfort is added right here. But on ordinary days the blessing isn't a lament. It's construction language. Rebuild. Sprout. Every day, a little more.
screen: `RETURN TO JERUSALEM IN MERCY.` · `WHO BUILDS: AN ONGOING ACT.` · `TZEMACH: THE BRANCH OF DAVID.` · `PRAY FOR THE PEACE OF JERUSALEM.` · then, large: `REBUILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope for one repair. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that's broken and could, slowly, be rebuilt. A relationship. A neighborhood. Your health after a hard year. Your trust in yourself. Don't plan the whole thing. Picture one brick: the first small piece that could go back in place. Hold the hope that it can be built, in its time. If you pray, you can join that hope to the prayer for Jerusalem. The bell holds the time.
Jerusalem rebuilt. The Amidah's fourteenth and fifteenth blessings: the city built in mercy, and the branch of David's line.
Your line: rebuild. Today, put the first brick back: one small act toward the repair you pictured. Day five hundred ninety-one.

592.title: Hear our prayer
592.hook: here any personal request may be added in your own words
592.howItsDone: Shome'a tefillah is the sixteenth blessing of the weekday Amidah; many Jews pause within it to add personal requests in their own words and language, and someone keeping a private fast adds the prayer Aneinu here.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the city that's always being built. Your line was rebuild. Did one brick go back in place? Today, the last of the requests, and the one with a blank space in it. Day five hundred ninety-two.

The Amidah's words are fixed. Jews in Tokyo and Toronto say nearly the same sentences, in the same order, three times a day. Which raises a fair question. What if what you actually need isn't on the list? A scholarship. The courage to leave a bad job. Your dog's surgery on Thursday. A sister who hasn't called back. The prayer has an answer for that, and it's built into the very last request.
screen: `AS FIXED AS A PRAYER GETS.` → `WHAT IF IT'S NOT ON THE LIST?` → `THE LAST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The sixteenth blessing says: hear our voice, Lord our God. Have pity and compassion on us, and accept our prayer with mercy and favor. Don't turn us away empty-handed, for You hear the prayer of every mouth. Blessed are You, who hears prayer. In Hebrew, shome'a tefillah. The Psalms put it this way, in the old Jewish translation: "O Thou that hearest prayer, unto Thee doth all flesh come." All flesh. Every mouth. Not only the eloquent, not only those who know the Hebrew. The Talmud, in Avodah Zarah 8a, records the rule: a person may ask for their own needs in this blessing. Any need. The fixed requests before it cover what a whole people needs, wisdom, forgiveness, healing, a good year, justice. This blessing leaves a gap for what only you need. And it doesn't have to be in Hebrew. The Mishnah already allows the Amidah to be said in any language a person understands, and personal additions are often whispered in whatever language the heart speaks first: English, Yiddish, Spanish, Russian, Amharic. Someone fasting privately adds a short prayer here too. It's like a long form of printed questions that ends with one open box: anything else? The rabbis built that box into the center of Jewish prayer. The tradition holds the words steady for everyone, and then, near the end, steps back and says: now, in your own words.
screen: `SHOME'A TEFILLAH: WHO HEARS PRAYER.` · `EVERY MOUTH, ALL FLESH.` · `ANY NEED MAY BE ADDED HERE.` · `IN ANY LANGUAGE.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WORDS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add one private request. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what you actually need right now, not what you think you should need. Let it be specific and a little embarrassing if it is: the exam, the bill, the conversation you're dreading, the loneliness on Sunday nights. Put it into one plain sentence, in whatever language comes first. If you pray, you can say it as a request. If not, simply say it to yourself, out loud or under your breath. The bell holds the time.
Hear our prayer. Shome'a tefillah. The Amidah's sixteenth blessing, where any personal request may be added, in any words.
Your line: your own words here. Today, write your one private request down somewhere only you'll see, and look at it once tonight. Day five hundred ninety-two.

593.title: We thank you
593.hook: everyone bows at "we give thanks"; the rabbis say this blessing is said by all
593.howItsDone: Jews bow at the beginning and end of Modim, the thanksgiving blessing of every Amidah; during the leader's repetition the congregation says Modim d'Rabbanan quietly, and on Hanukkah and Purim the paragraph Al hanissim is added.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blank space in the Amidah. Your line was your own words here. Did you write your private request down? Today, the asking is over, and the thanks begins. Day five hundred ninety-three.

When the leader repeats the Amidah out loud, the congregation mostly listens. They answer amen at the end of each blessing, and let the leader speak for them. You can ask on someone's behalf. You can be represented. Then the leader reaches one blessing, bows, and the whole room does something different. Everyone starts murmuring their own words, at the same time, quietly, as if to say: no, this one, I'll do myself.
screen: `THE ROOM LISTENS AND ANSWERS AMEN.` → `ONE BLESSING, EVERYONE BOWS.` → `THIS ONE, I'LL DO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: After a short blessing asking that prayer be accepted, called Retzeh, comes the eighteenth: Modim. It begins: we thank You, for You are the Lord our God and the God of our ancestors forever. Then it lists: for our lives, entrusted to Your hand. For our souls, in Your keeping. For Your miracles that are with us every day, and Your wonders and goodness at every time: evening, morning and noon. Not the parting of the sea. The miracles of every day. People bow at its first word and at its end, as they did at the start of the Amidah. And when the leader repeats it aloud, the congregation says its own quiet version, called Modim d'Rabbanan, the Modim of the rabbis. The Talmud, in Sotah 40a, collects the different words several rabbis said here, and later commentators explain why everyone joins in: someone else can make a request for you, but no one can say thank you on your behalf. The word itself, modim, can mean both we thank and we acknowledge. In Genesis, when Leah has her fourth son, she says, in the old Jewish translation: "This time will I praise the LORD." And she names him Yehudah, Judah. The word Jew, tradition notes, goes back to Judah. So in a sense, the very name of the people is a thank-you. On Hanukkah and Purim, a special paragraph about those miracles is added right here.
screen: `FOR OUR LIVES, IN YOUR HAND.` · `MIRACLES EVERY DAY: EVENING, MORNING, NOON.` · `NO ONE CAN THANK FOR YOU.` · `MODIM: THANK AND ACKNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `WE THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow slightly in thanks. Sit or stand, and breathe. Think of three ordinary things from today: one from the morning, one from the afternoon, one from now. A cup of coffee, a message from a friend, the fact that your lungs are doing this without being asked. For each one, bow your head slightly. Just a small nod, the way you might to someone across a room. If you pray, you can say: we thank You. The bell holds the time.
Modim. We thank, we acknowledge. The Amidah's thanksgiving blessing, said with a bow, by everyone in their own words.
Your line: we thank you. Today, thank one person yourself, directly, instead of letting someone else pass it on. Day five hundred ninety-three.

594.title: Grant peace
594.hook: the Amidah ends asking for peace, goodness and blessing
594.howItsDone: Sim Shalom is the final blessing of the Amidah, following the priestly blessing in the morning repetition; many Ashkenazi communities say the shorter Shalom Rav at the afternoon and evening services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Modim, the thanks no one can say for you. Your line was we thank you. Did you thank someone yourself? Today, the last blessing of the Amidah. Day five hundred ninety-four.

Think of how many things end on peace. Shalom is the word for hello and for goodbye. The Kaddish ends on it. So does the priestly blessing from the book of Numbers. Even the Mishnah, the great code of Jewish law, sixty-three tractates of rules about fields, festivals, courts and purity, closes its very last page with a sentence about peace. The Amidah follows the same pattern. After praise, after thirteen requests, after thanks, the very last thing it asks for is shalom.
screen: `HELLO, GOODBYE: SHALOM.` → `THE MISHNAH'S LAST PAGE.` → `THE AMIDAH'S LAST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: In the leader's morning repetition, just before this blessing, comes the priestly blessing. In the old Jewish translation, it ends: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." In Israel, descendants of the priests, kohanim, come forward and say it every day; in many communities outside Israel, they do so on festivals. Then the last blessing picks up the thread: Sim shalom. Grant peace, goodness and blessing, grace, kindness and compassion, to us and to all Your people Israel. Bless us, our Father, all of us as one, with the light of Your face. Blessed are You, who blesses Your people Israel with peace. The light of Your face is borrowed straight from the priestly blessing before it. All of us as one: peace is something no one can have alone. Shalom comes from a root meaning whole, complete. It's not only the absence of fighting. It's nothing missing. In many Ashkenazi communities, the afternoon and evening services use a shorter version, Shalom Rav, abundant peace. And that sentence on the Mishnah's last page? Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta says that God found no vessel that could hold blessing except peace, and quotes the Psalm: "the LORD will bless His people with peace." A vessel: all the other blessings, health, livelihood, wisdom, leak out without it. So the Amidah puts the container last, to hold everything that came before.
screen: `THE PRIESTLY BLESSING: GIVE THEE PEACE.` · `ALL OF US AS ONE.` · `SHALOM: WHOLE, NOTHING MISSING.` · `THE ONLY VESSEL THAT HOLDS BLESSING.` · then, large: `GRANT PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish peace on one person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose life feels un-whole right now: someone grieving, someone in a fight, someone pulled in too many directions. Picture them clearly. On each out-breath, send them one piece of what's missing: rest, calm, a quiet evening, a phone call that goes well. If you pray, you can ask for their shalom. If it's someone you're in conflict with, notice whether you can wish it for them too. The bell holds the time.
Sim Shalom. Grant peace. The Amidah's final blessing: peace, goodness and blessing, for all of us as one.
Your line: grant peace. Today, do one thing that makes something in someone's life more whole: finish what you promised, fix what you broke, or simply show up. Day five hundred ninety-four.

595.title: Guard my tongue (Berakhot 17a)
595.hook: the closing prayer: my God, guard my tongue from evil
595.howItsDone: After the final blessing of the Amidah, Jews say Elohai netzor quietly, then Psalm 19:15, then take three steps back, bow left, right and center while saying oseh shalom, and stand a moment before stepping forward again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sim Shalom, the vessel that holds every blessing. Your line was grant peace. Did you make one thing more whole? Today, the very last words before the three steps back. Day five hundred ninety-five.

A small experiment for the end of the day: count the things said about people who weren't in the room. The coworker's annoying habit. The friend's bad decision. The relative everyone sighs about. The tally can climb fast. Now look at where the Amidah puts its last request. The person praying has stood for several minutes, feet together, asking for wisdom, healing and peace. And as they get ready to step back into the day, the closing prayer worries first about one thing: the mouth.
screen: `COUNT WHAT GETS SAID ABOUT PEOPLE.` → `THE TALLY CLIMBS FAST.` → `THE LAST WORRY: THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot 16b and 17a, records the private prayers different rabbis said after they finished the Amidah. One of them, from Mar the son of Ravina, is the one printed in the prayer book today. It begins: Elohai, netzor leshoni mera. My God, guard my tongue from evil, and my lips from speaking deceit. It's built on a psalm. In the old Jewish translation: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." Then it goes on: to those who curse me, let my soul be silent; let my soul be like dust to everyone. Open my heart to Your Torah. Notice the grammar has changed. The Amidah's requests speak as we: heal us, forgive us, bring us back. This prayer suddenly says my. My tongue. My soul. It began as one rabbi's personal prayer, and it still sounds like one. It ends with another psalm: "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before Thee, O LORD, my Rock, and my Redeemer." Then the three steps back, a bow to the left, the right and the center, and oseh shalom: may the one who makes peace on high make peace for us. Remember three steps in, and open my lips? The Amidah opened by asking God to open the mouth. It closes by asking God to guard it. Between those two requests, the whole prayer: ancestors, power, holiness, thirteen requests, thanks and peace.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your tongue for an hour. Settle, and breathe. Pick the next hour of your day that will have people in it: a meeting, a family dinner, a group chat. Decide now: for that one hour, nothing unkind about someone who isn't there. No eye-rolls, no small digs. Picture the moment the temptation will come, and the quiet you'll put in its place. If you pray, you can say the first line: my God, guard my tongue from evil. The bell holds the time.
Elohai Netzor. My God, guard. The personal prayer after the Amidah, asking to guard the tongue from evil.

Your line: guard my tongue. A week that prayed against harm, for the ones who chose, for Jerusalem, in our own words, with thanks, for peace, and now for a guarded tongue. That's the whole Amidah walked. Today, keep your one guarded hour. Day five hundred ninety-five.
